Finland built a lighthouse on the shared islet of Märket in 1885. What went wrong?
It ended up on the Swedish side
It was built facing the wrong way
It was two metres too short
The builders picked the highest rock, which happened to lie across the border.
In 1985 the Finland-Sweden border on Märket was redrawn into which shape?
The S-bend hands the lighthouse to Finland and gives Sweden an equal piece elsewhere on the rock.
What rule did the 1985 redrawing of the Märket border have to obey?
Finland had to pay for the land
The border had to stay straight
Both halves had to be equal
Area and coastline had to come out even, so neither state gained territory or fishing water.
Why are Märket's border markers holes drilled into the rock?
Drift ice would shear off anything standing
The rock is too hard for posts
Birds knocked the old posts over
Paint does not stick to the stone
Winter ice scours the whole islet, so a marker that sticks up does not survive.
Märket was probably under water until the 1500s. Why is it dry land now?
The land is still rising after the ice age
Sand has piled up on it
A storm raised the sea bed
Fennoscandia is rebounding from the weight of the ice sheet, so new rock keeps emerging.
Which municipality owns the Finnish half of Märket?
The islet's Finnish side belongs to Hammarland in Åland; the Swedish side is split between two counties.
Märket, about three hectares, holds which record?
Smallest sea island split between two states
Smallest island with a post office
Roughly 350 by 150 metres, and a national border runs right across it.
Madha is an Omani exclave inside the UAE. What sits inside Madha?
A piece of Oman's other half
A stretch of no man's land
The village of Nahwa belongs to the UAE, so it is a country inside a country inside a country.
Which Spanish region keeps an exclave, Treviño, inside the Basque province of Alava?
About 280 square kilometres of Castile and Leon sit entirely surrounded by Basque territory.
How does Bangladesh reach its exclave of Dahagram-Angarpota?
Along a leased corridor through India
By a tunnel under Indian soil
By a bridge over Indian soil
The Tin Bigha corridor, about 85 metres wide, is leased from India for the purpose.
Which German city-state is made of two parts, each surrounded by Lower Saxony?
Bremen and Bremerhaven are each an enclave of Lower Saxony and an exclave of the other.
Two Italian villages, Grimacco and Drenchia, share which odd arrangement?
Each is an enclave inside the other
Their territories interlock so that each municipality encloses a piece of its neighbour.
The Japanese town of Fujiyoshida keeps an exclave where?
On the summit of Mount Fuji
On an island in Tokyo Bay
On the slopes of Mount Aso
A shrine high on Fuji belongs to Fujiyoshida although neighbouring land does not.
Which Russian republic is almost entirely surrounded by Krasnodar Krai?
Adygea is a republic in its own right but sits as an enclave inside a single Russian region.
Fahr Abbey in Switzerland had an unusual legal status until 2007. What was it?
It was in two countries at once
From 1803 to 2007 the monastery sat outside every commune, answering to the canton alone.
The Peanut Hole is a pocket of high seas enclosed by one country's waters. Which sea?
Russia's economic zone surrounds it on every side, so it is international water with no coast.
The Cypriot village of Ormidhia is completely surrounded by what?
It is an exclave of the Republic of Cyprus inside the Sovereign Base Area of Dhekelia.
Which Norwegian town owns Himberg, an exclave inside neighbouring Larvik?
Nordic municipal borders were drawn from old farm holdings, which left scattered pieces behind.
Which capital city has two of its three parts as enclaves in a surrounding province?
Mongolia's capital is split into three, and two of the pieces sit inside Tov province.
A 1914 seawall left the original Ellis Island surrounded by which state?
Landfill joined the island to New Jersey water, but the old core stayed under New York.
Hans Island lies between Greenland and which Canadian island?
The Kennedy Channel runs between them, and the 1973 sea boundary cut straight through the island.
Sarvan is a long, narrow strip of which country reaching into Uzbekistan?
Soviet planners drew borders round villages and irrigation, not round nations.
Before 2022 Denmark had a land border with only one country. Which?
Jutland touches only Germany, so the Hans Island deal gave Denmark a second land neighbour.
Which treaty first demilitarised the Åland Islands?
Britain and France had destroyed the Russian fort of Bomarsund, and the peace barred rebuilding.
Why are men from Åland exempt from Finnish conscription?
They serve in the Swedish army instead
They pay a special tax instead
Åland has its own small army
A demilitarised territory has no garrison, so the duty to serve was dropped with it.
Åland has an ISO country code of its own, separate from Finland's. Which?
The code brought the islands their own internet domain, .ax, alongside Finland's .fi.
What does Åland's right of domicile allow that Finnish citizenship alone does not?
Voting in Åland and owning rural land
A second vote in Finnish elections
It is inherited or earned in five years, and Finland's EU accession deal protects it.
How many seats does Åland hold in the Finnish parliament?
The islands have their own parliament for their own affairs, and a single national seat.
In the 1919 petition, roughly what share of Åland's voters asked to join Sweden?
Finland refused and offered autonomy instead; the League of Nations settled it in 1921.
Sokh is an Uzbek enclave inside Kyrgyzstan. What is unexpected about its people?
Almost all of them are Tajik
Soviet borders followed canals and collective farms, not the languages people spoke.
What did Norwegians campaign to give Finland for its centenary of independence?
Moving the border about 200 metres would have made Halti's peak Finland's highest point.
How much new land does Finland gain each year from the land still rising?
The crust is rebounding from the ice sheet, fastest in the northern Gulf of Bothnia.
Which river was born when a tilting lake broke through the Uimaharju esker?
Land uplift tipped the lake until it cut a new outlet for itself through the ridge.
Which Swedish lake was cut off from the sea by land uplift and turned fresh?
It closed off around the 12th century, and Stockholm was founded at the new outlet.
Why have the harbours of Tornio and Pori each been moved several times?
The land keeps rising and the sea retreats
Ships grew too large for them
In the northern Baltic the shoreline walks seawards, so a quay silts up within generations.
In Finland, who owns land that newly rises out of the water?
The owner of the former water area
New shore follows the old water title, and the shore landowner may buy it at market price.
Where in the Baltic is the land rising fastest, about 11 millimetres a year?
That is where the ice was thickest, so the crust there has the most rebounding left to do.
The Quitasueño banks became enclaves of which country inside Nicaragua's waters?
A court gave Nicaragua the sea but left Colombia the banks, creating islands of jurisdiction.
Why do the ferries between Finland and Sweden all stop at Mariehamn or Långnäs?
Åland lies outside the EU VAT area, so a call there keeps duty-free selling legal.
Which 1920 treaty gave every signatory equal mining rights on a Norwegian archipelago?
Norway got sovereignty, but all parties kept the right to fish, hunt, mine and trade there.
What may taxes collected on Svalbard be spent on?
The treaty ties the money to the archipelago, which is why income tax there is low.
Which inhabited archipelago can citizens of any country enter without a visa?
The 1920 treaty's equal-access rule has been read as making the whole place visa-free.
Which country besides Norway has run coal towns on Svalbard for decades?
Barentsburg and Pyramiden were worked under the treaty's equal mining rights.
Saudi Arabia joined the Svalbard Treaty in 1925 under which name?
Parties joined as the states they then were, so the list preserves several vanished countries.
How long after signing the treaty did Norway rename Spitsbergen to Svalbard?
The name changed in 1925, when Norwegian rule over the archipelago actually took effect.
Which French king's reign lasted about twenty minutes?
During the July Revolution of 1830 he held the crown only long enough to abdicate.
Luís Filipe of Portugal reigned for about twenty minutes in 1908. Why?
He was hurt in the attack that killed his father
Father and son were shot in Lisbon, and the son outlived his father by minutes.
Which monarch of England reigned for nine days in 1553?
She was proclaimed, then deposed, because the country backed Henry VIII's daughter instead.
Edward V of England reigned 77 days. How did his reign end?
He was deposed and vanished in the Tower
He abdicated in favour of his brother
He was crowned in France instead
His uncle took the throne as Richard III, and the boy was never seen again.
Why did Michael II of Russia's reign in 1917 last less than a day?
He would take the throne only if an assembly elected him, so he never actually reigned.
Pedro IV of Portugal reigned 53 days in 1826 and then abdicated in favour of whom?
He was already emperor of Brazil, and the two crowns could not be held together.
Yuan Shikai's 81-day Chinese empire of 1916 ended how?
He handed it to a child emperor
The restoration proved so unpopular that the republic was put back within three months.
In 1918 the Finnish parliament elected a king. Who was he?
The vote was meant to cement the alliance with Imperial Germany, which had backed the Whites.
Why did Finland's elected king of 1918 never take the throne?
He was already a king elsewhere
With the Central Powers beaten, a German-born king of Finland was suddenly impossible.
How could the Finnish parliament of 1918 vote for a monarchy at all?
Its socialist members had been removed
The vote needed only a third
The vote was taken in secret
After the civil war the chamber was purged, which left a monarchist majority.
In 1742 the Finnish estates met in Turku and asked a Russian ruler for a king. Who?
Russia was occupying Finland, and the estates proposed Duke Peter of Holstein-Gottorp as king.
Which Swedish king briefly styled himself King of the Finns?
He used the title between 1607 and 1611, with no effect on anyone's actual status.
Which country once had a 30 February in its calendar?
An extra leap day in 1712 undid an earlier botched attempt at calendar reform.
Why did Sweden add a 30 February in 1712?
To get back to the Julian calendar
To fix an error by its astronomers
Sweden had dropped the leap day in 1700 to reform gradually, then gave up and put it back.
How many days did the Swedish year 1712 have?
A leap year plus one extra day of correction, so February ran to the thirtieth.
Sweden finally adopted the Gregorian calendar in 1753 by doing what?
Eleven days were dropped in one go, a century after most of Catholic Europe had switched.
In 1845 Finland was the only country in the world to do what?
Finland had kept the Swedish astronomical Easter rule after being severed from Sweden in 1809.
Which war between the Netherlands and the Isles of Scilly ran for 335 years?
The Three Hundred and Thirty Five Years' War
The War of the Narrow Seas
Admiral Tromp declared it in 1651 over Royalist raiding, and nobody ever signed a peace.
How many casualties did the 335 years' war with the Isles of Scilly cause?
Not a shot was fired: the Royalist fleet surrendered to others and the Dutch sailed home.
Why did the war with the Isles of Scilly last so long on paper?
The 1654 peace treaty never mentioned it
The Dutch kept a blockade going
Both sides forgot who had declared it
The Treaty of Westminster ended the Anglo-Dutch war but said nothing of this separate quarrel.
In which year was peace finally declared with the Isles of Scilly?
A local historian wrote to the Dutch embassy, which confirmed no treaty had ever been signed.
The Åland Convention of 1921 was the League of Nations' first what?
The League let Finland keep the islands but bound it to grant autonomy and neutrality.
In the Whisky War over Hans Island, what did Canadian soldiers leave behind?
Each visit swapped the flag and the drink, which is how a border dispute stayed friendly.
What did Denmark's minister leave on Hans Island in reply in 1984?
The note read 'Welcome to the Danish island', and the exchange carried on for decades.
A 1937 German decree barred Germans from accepting Nobel Prizes. What prompted it?
A German pacifist won the Peace Prize
The prize money was in foreign currency
Carl von Ossietzky, imprisoned in Germany, had been given the 1935 Peace Prize.
Who was the first person forced to decline a Nobel Prize?
The Gestapo arrested him and made him refuse the 1939 medicine prize by letter.
Who declined the Nobel Prize in Literature entirely of his own accord in 1964?
He held that a writer should not let himself be turned into an institution.
What result did Sweden's 1955 referendum on driving on the right give?
83 per cent wanted to keep left
A narrow win for the right
Parliament switched sides anyway in 1963, with effect from 1967.
Swedish cars were already left-hand drive before 1967. Why did that force a change?
Overtaking on narrow roads was dangerous
The cars could not be registered
A driver sitting away from the centre line cannot see past the vehicle in front.
Which Nordic country acceded to the Svalbard Treaty only in 1994?
The other Nordic states were among the fourteen original signatories of 1920.
Which Danish Nobel laureate's prize-winning discovery was later discredited?
He was given the 1926 medicine prize for a worm he believed caused cancer.
The Torres Strait Islands include seven Australian enclaves inside whose waters?
The border was drawn to keep the islanders Australian, so it runs close to the PNG coast.
Japan's economic zone completely encloses a pocket of high seas. Roughly how large?
Scattered islands throw out zones that meet around a gap no coast reaches.
Manila South Cemetery is surrounded by, and divided by, which neighbouring city?
The graveyard belongs to Manila but lies wholly outside it, cut in two by the city around it.
In 1709 Sweden's Easter fell how far from the Gregorian date?
Sweden applied Julian Easter rules to a calendar that was one day out of step with both.
Which Finnish party had members propose restoring the monarchy as late as 2014?
The idea got no support at all, which is why almost nobody remembers it happened.
Halley's Comet had been seen for centuries. What did Halley actually do?
Worked out its orbit and predicted its return
Saw it first through a telescope
Chinese records go back to 240 BC; Halley was the first to show the visits were one comet.
Arabic numerals are named after the Arabs. Where were they actually developed?
Indian mathematicians worked them out; Arab scholars carried them to Europe, and got the name.
The Archimedes screw predates Archimedes by centuries. Who used it first?
It was raising water in Mesopotamia some three hundred years before he was born.
Who put Maxwell's equations into the four-equation form we learn today?
Maxwell wrote twenty equations in twenty variables; Heaviside boiled them down to four.
Which of Newton's three laws of motion was genuinely his own?
Galileo, Hooke and Huygens had the first two in hand; action and reaction was Newton's.
Who published the bell curve in 1733, long before Gauss gave it his name?
He found it while studying coin tosses, sixty years before Gauss began using it.
Venn diagrams carry Venn's name, but who introduced them?
Euler used overlapping circles in 1768; Venn systematised them a century later.
Who first described Gresham's law - in the very year Gresham was born?
Copernicus set it out in 1519, and the man it is named after was born that same year.
Who invented the Playfair cipher, which bears Lord Playfair's name?
Wheatstone devised it in 1854; Playfair simply promoted it to the government.
The Wheatstone bridge was invented by whom, ten years before Wheatstone used it?
Christie published it in 1833; Wheatstone made it famous in 1843 and kept the credit.
Who is believed to have discovered the rule we call L'Hôpital's rule?
L'Hôpital paid Bernoulli for his mathematical discoveries and published them as his own.
Who designed and built the balance that measured gravity, named after Cavendish?
Michell died before he could use it, and the apparatus passed to Cavendish.
Pythagoras' theorem was in use long before him. By whom?
Clay tablets show the relation in use more than a thousand years earlier.
Who invented the Ising model of magnetism and handed it to Ising to work on?
Lenz devised it and gave it to his doctoral student, whose name it now carries.
The Yagi-Uda television aerial is usually just called a Yagi. Who invented it?
Uda did the work; Yagi translated and promoted it abroad, so the short name stuck to him.
The impossible Penrose triangle was drawn decades earlier by which Swede?
Reutersvärd drew it in 1934; Penrose arrived at the same figure in the 1950s.
Which Estonian astronomer proposed the Oort cloud 28 years before Oort?
Öpik's 1932 paper described the distant comet reservoir; Oort came to it in 1960.
Who derived the relation we call Hubble's law, two years before Hubble?
Lemaître published it in 1927 in a little-read Belgian journal.
The Liebig condenser is named after Liebig, who denied inventing it. Which Finn built one?
Gadolin was one of several who had the same device working before Liebig popularised it.
Who worked out the fast Fourier transform algorithm, in 1805?
Gauss used it for asteroid orbits; it was rediscovered and named in 1965.
Gerard Kuiper did not believe in the Kuiper belt. What did he think?
That such a belt no longer existed
That it was made of gas
That it lay inside Jupiter's orbit
That it was a single large planet
He argued any such disc of bodies would long since have been swept away.
Whose names were left out of the report that gave us the von Neumann architecture?
The 1945 draft circulated with von Neumann's name alone on the front page.
Stigler's law says things are named after the wrong person. Whom did Stigler name it after?
He credited Merton on purpose, so that his own law would be an example of itself.
Fermi's golden rule in quantum physics was derived by whom?
Dirac worked it out; Fermi called it a golden rule in his lectures and the name stuck.
Who gave an early warning of what we now call the Dunning-Kruger effect?
Russell wrote that the stupid are cocksure while the intelligent are full of doubt.
Poisson's bright spot is named after a man who used it to ridicule which idea?
That light has a finite speed
He said a wave theory would absurdly put a bright dot in a shadow's centre - and there it was.
The Arrhenius equation bears a Swedish name. Who proposed it, in 1884?
Van 't Hoff proposed the form; Arrhenius supplied the physical explanation five years later.
Snell's law of refraction was found six centuries earlier by whom?
The Baghdad scholar wrote it down about 984, long before Snellius restated it.
Who discovered the steelmaking process patented by Bessemer?
Kelly found it in 1851 in Kentucky; Bessemer patented it in Britain four years later.
Who actually first proved the theorem known as Stokes's theorem?
Kelvin found it and mentioned it in a letter; Stokes set it as an exam question.
Which element is named after the Norse god of thunder?
Berzelius named it for Thor after the mineral thorite found in Norway.
Niels Bohr's institute identified an element in 1923 and named it after its own city. Which?
Hafnia is the Latin name of Copenhagen, where the work was done.
Why does sodium have the symbol Na?
From the Greek word for salt
Chemical symbols were fixed from Latin names, which English later stopped using.
Tungsten has the symbol W. Where does the letter come from?
German chemistry called it wolfram, while Swedish gave English tungsten, heavy stone.
What gave Alfred Nobel the idea for blasting gelatin?
The dressing on a cut finger
Collodion put on the wound showed him how to combine his two explosives safely.
How did Pasteur stumble on the first deliberately made vaccine?
An assistant left a culture to age over a holiday
The weakened old culture failed to kill the chickens and then protected them.
Newton was at home when the apple fell. Why was he not at his university?
It had closed because of plague
He had quarrelled with his tutor
Cambridge shut during the plague years, which gave him two years of undisturbed thinking.
How did Pasteur notice that identical molecules can be mirror images?
A solution crystallised oddly on a cold windowsill
He compared two acids by taste
He dropped a crystal and it split
The cold Paris night sorted the crystals into two forms he could pick apart by hand.
Why can a Nobel science prize go to at most three people?
A limit the committee added itself
The prize money divides by three
The will sets no such limit; the rule now leaves out members of large collaborations.
Why is there no Nobel Prize in mathematics?
Sweden already had a maths academy
The rival-in-love story cannot be true, as Nobel never married.
Dmitri Mendeleev never won a Nobel Prize. How close did he come?
He lost by one vote in 1906
He won it but it was withdrawn
He died the following year, and the prize cannot be awarded after death.
Why did one Nobel committee telephone a carpet cleaner in 1987?
The cleaner shared the laureate's address
Donald Cram was the chemistry winner; somebody with a similar name picked up.
Raymond Chandler left Poodle Springs four chapters long. Who finished it?
Thirty-one pages existed; Parker wrote the rest and the estate published it as a novel.
How much of The Mystery of Edwin Drood did Dickens live to publish?
He died with the solution unwritten, which is why dozens of endings have been attempted.
Who completed Arthur C. Clarke's last novel, The Last Theorem?
Clarke read and approved the finished manuscript only days before he died.
Spider Robinson built the novel Variable Star from how much Heinlein material?
Seven of an eight-page outline survived, and the rest of the book was written around them.
Jack London wrote 20,000 words of The Assassination Bureau and then stopped. Why?
He could not find a logical ending
He was taken to court over it
Robert L. Fish finished it half a century later from London's own notes.
Which Jane Austen fragment of eleven chapters has been completed by many hands?
She was dying as she wrote it, and the unfinished text has invited continuations ever since.
Who finished Michael Crichton's Micro from a manuscript found on his computer?
A second unfinished Crichton book, Eruption, was later completed by James Patterson.
Which nearly complete Dumas novel was rediscovered in 1990 and then finished?
Claude Schopp found it serialised in old newspapers and wrote the missing ending.
Who wrote the last six chapters of Robert Louis Stevenson's St Ives?
Stevenson died in Samoa in 1894 with the novel unfinished.
How did Walter Besant finish Wilkie Collins's last novel, Blind Love?
Collins had written out the plot of the final third before he became too ill to write it.
Who finished The Guernsey Literary and Potato Peel Pie Society?
Mary Ann Shaffer's health failed, and Annie Barrows completed the book as co-author.
Which Finnish writer published under both Maiju Lassila and Irmari Rantamala?
He used at least four names, and the two best known were a woman's and a man's.
Tove Jansson published one picture book under which pen name?
Everything else carried her own name, so the one disguised book is easily missed.
Which Finnish folklorist published his poetry as P. Mustapää?
He kept the scholar and the poet apart under two names for his whole career.
Hella Wuolijoki wrote plays under which man's name?
The Estonian-born playwright used a Finnish male pen name for her best-known work.
Simo Puupponen wrote his humorous columns under which single name?
The name became better known than his own, and his books still carry it.
Vihtori Peltonen is remembered by which pen name?
The author of Laulu tulipunaisesta kukasta took a name from a lake and a brook.
Karen Blixen wrote Out of Africa under which name?
A woman writing memoir under a man's first name reached an English readership more easily.
Which pen name did Stephen King use until a bookshop clerk unmasked him?
He wanted to know whether the books sold on their merits or on his name.
J. K. Rowling's The Cuckoo's Calling first appeared under which name?
She wanted the crime novels judged without the expectations her own name brought.
How did Romain Gary become the only writer to win the Prix Goncourt twice?
He entered under a pen name
The prize can be won only once, so his second win came as Émile Ajar.
Agatha Christie's romantic novels appeared under which name?
Readers who wanted detective stories would not have bought them from her own name.
Sylvia Plath's The Bell Jar was first published under which name?
The novel drew so closely on her own life that she did not want it under her name.
The author of the Tibetan memoir The Third Eye turned out to be what?
Cyril Hoskin had never been to Tibet, and his books sold on anyway.
Benjamin Franklin's first newspaper columns were signed with whose name?
His brother ran the paper and would not print him, so he slid the letters under the door.
Why was Little Black Sambo banned in Japan from 1988?
To head off boycott threats against Japanese exports
A court ruled on the illustrations
The pressure came from abroad, and the ban lasted until 2005.
For what occasion did Sibelius write the music that became Finlandia?
The opening of the national theatre
The tableaux were a protest against Russian press censorship, dressed as a history pageant.
Who wrote the Finnish words to the Finlandia hymn, in 1941?
Sibelius wrote the tune without words; the text came four decades later.
Which short-lived African state used the Finlandia hymn as its national anthem?
The breakaway state took a Finnish tune of resistance and set English words to it.
The Finlandia hymn is often called a folk melody. Why is that wrong?
It is a Russian marching song
It is a Swedish drinking song
The hymn section is his own invention, not a tune he collected.
Finland shares its national anthem's melody with which country?
Both nations took Fredrik Pacius's tune, and Estonia restored it on regaining independence.
Which country's anthem is sung to the tune of God Save the King?
Oben am jungen Rhein uses the same melody, which has been shared since 1920.
Greece shares its national anthem word for word with which country?
Cyprus adopted the Hymn to Liberty in 1966, text and all.
Why did the United Arab Emirates ban Animal Farm from schools?
A talking pig was held to clash with Islamic values
The 2002 ban rested on the animals rather than on the politics of the book.
Alice's Adventures in Wonderland was banned in Hunan in 1931. On what grounds?
It was thought to be code
A provincial governor held that putting human speech in animals degraded people.
Why did the US defence department buy up and destroy 9,500 copies of a memoir?
It was printed on the wrong paper
The author had not been paid
A redacted second edition of Operation Dark Heart was published instead.
Which Nabokov novel was banned in Britain from 1955 to 1959?
France had allowed it from 1958 but still forbade displaying it in shop windows.
Henry Miller's Tropic of Cancer reached English readers through which city?
Obelisk Press printed English books in France that could not be sold at home.
Why did Guatemala ban Mein Kampf together with anti-Hitler books?
To look neutral in the war
Banning both sides was presented as even-handedness while the war went on.
Which Norwegian novel's ban was lifted in 1958, two years after it appeared?
The Song of the Red Ruby
Agnar Mykle's novel went to court for obscenity and was cleared on appeal.
Why was the children's book Snorri the Seal banned in Norway in 1941?
It was read as a satire of the occupation
A harmless-looking animal fable was understood by everybody as a political one.
Doctor Zhivago was banned in the Soviet Union. What did the pressure cost its author?
He had to reject his Nobel Prize
He was barred from writing poetry
Boris Pasternak was honoured posthumously in 1989, three decades later.
The memoir Spycatcher was banned in Britain at an unusual moment. When?
The ban made the Australian edition famous and copies were carried in by travellers.
Why were women barred from Olympic races longer than 200 metres until 1960?
Officials took the exhausted finishers as proof the distance was unsuitable for women.
Why was Paavo Nurmi barred from the 1932 Olympic marathon?
Travel money and training expenses were enough for the federation to call him paid.
What did Finland do in protest after Nurmi's 1932 ban?
Stopped its athletics meetings against Sweden
The annual Finland-Sweden match was not held again until 1939.
Which Finnish speed skater refused to compete at Lake Placid in 1932?
The Americans ran all six skaters at once instead of in pairs, which he would not accept.
Why did the 1948 St Moritz Olympics have two American ice hockey teams?
Two rival federations each sent one
A team arrived a week late
One was made up of exiles
The IOC barred both, the Swiss let one play, and a year later that one was disqualified too.
Finland competed separately from Russia at Stockholm in 1912, but could not do what?
Finnish gold medallists had to stand under the Russian flag.
Which Swede refused his silver medal when Jim Thorpe's gold was taken away?
He said the decathlon had been won by Thorpe and he would not take the title.
Why were Jim Thorpe's 1912 Olympic golds stripped?
He had been paid to play baseball
He had competed for two countries
Two summers of minor-league pay made him a professional under the rules of the day.
How did Frederick Lorz come to lead the 1904 Olympic marathon?
He rode much of it in a car
He swapped numbers with a team-mate
He had dropped out, got a lift, rejoined at nineteen miles and jogged in first.
Why was Spyridon Belokas disqualified from the 1896 marathon?
He covered part of the course by carriage
He started from the wrong place
He admitted the ride and the third place was taken from him.
Why was the 1908 Olympic 400 metres final a walkover for Wyndham Halswelle?
The others refused to run the rerun
The others had already won medals
An American was disqualified for blocking, legal at home but not in Britain, and his team walked.
Where were the swimming events of the 1900 Paris Olympics held?
In the sea at Le Havre
The river also carried the city's sewage, which the swimmers had to put up with.
Which Swedish rider was demoted to last place in the 1932 Olympic dressage?
Judges heard clicking they took for encouraging the horse, which the rules forbade.
What did Sandström say had made the clicking sound in the 1932 dressage?
The explanation did not save him, and the demotion stood.
What did the 1952 Oslo Winter Olympics introduce for bobsleigh?
Crews had been picked for sheer mass, so a 400 kilogram ceiling was set.
Which Swede was the first athlete disqualified from the Olympics for a banned substance?
He had drunk two beers to steady his hand before the pentathlon shooting in 1968.
What substance cost Sweden its 1968 modern pentathlon bronze?
Alcohol was on the first banned list, because it steadies a shooter's hand.
Why were the equestrian events of the 1956 Melbourne Olympics held in Stockholm?
Horses could not be brought into Australia, so one sport was held on another continent.
Why did Peter O'Connor climb a flagpole at the 1906 Games?
He was listed as British, not Irish
His medal was given to another
He wanted to fix the flag
He waved an Irish flag from the top while a team-mate guarded the pole.
Boris Onishchenko was disqualified at the 1976 Olympics for what?
A rigged epee with a hidden switch
The weapon could register a hit that had never landed, and his whole team went out.
Why did Innsbruck host the 1976 Winter Olympics instead of Denver?
A referendum made Colorado the only place to hand the Games back after winning them.
Why did Taiwan's team march at Rome in 1960 carrying a sign reading 'Under Protest'?
It was made to compete as Formosa
